claims.claim: Moses and Aaron demand, "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness" (5:1).

Pharaoh replies, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the LORD, neither will I let Israel go" (5:2) — ignorance and defiance in one sentence, which the plagues then answer (see conn-pl-002).
The demand is for a three-days' journey into the wilderness to sacrifice (5:3), the same request made at the burning bush (Ex 3:18; see conn-pl-001).
Pharaoh accuses Moses and Aaron of letting the people "from their works" and calls the people idle (5:4–5, 17).
Pharaoh withholds straw while demanding "the same tale of bricks" (5:7–9); the work is to be "more" laid upon the men (*kaved*, the same root as the "heavy" heart — see clm-pl-028).
claims.evidence: Ex 5:7–9; BDB H3513 (Qal 1, "of work laid upon one, bondage," Ex 5:9).

claims.claim: The Hebrew officers (*shoterim*) are beaten by the taskmasters for failing the quota (5:14).
The officers appeal to Pharaoh, are told the people are idle, and leave "in evil case" (5:15–19).
The people turn on Moses and Aaron: "The LORD look upon you, and judge; because ye have made our savour to be abhorred in the eyes of Pharaoh" (5:20–21).

Moses complains to the LORD, "why is it that thou hast sent me? ... neither hast thou delivered thy people at all" (5:22–23); the increased burden is the immediate consequence of the first confrontation, and the people's despair is the narrative's starting point for the renewed promise of Ex 6.
"Now shalt thou see what I will do to Pharaoh: for with a strong hand shall he let them go" (6:1).

"I am the LORD: and I appeared unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, by the name of God Almighty, but by my name JEHOVAH was I not known to them" (6:2–3). The text states it; what "not known" means (the patriarchs knew the name, Gen 15:7, but not its redemptive content, or not its full significance) is debated among commentators and is not resolved here.
God reaffirms the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and says He has heard the groaning of Israel (6:4–5).
The deliverance promise of 6:6–8 is a sevenfold "I will": bring out, rid, redeem, take, be your God, bring in, give.
The people "hearkened not unto Moses for anguish of spirit, and for cruel bondage" (6:9).
Moses twice pleads inadequacy: "I am of uncircumcised lips" (6:12, 30), framing the commission (6:12) and its resumption (6:30).

Ex 6:14–27 traces Reuben, Simeon, and Levi down to Amram and Jochebed and their sons Moses and Aaron, closing, "these are that Aaron and Moses, to whom the LORD said, Bring out the children of Israel from the land of Egypt" (6:26).

The genealogy interrupts the commission narrative (6:13 breaks off; 6:28 resumes, "on the day when the LORD spake unto Moses in the land of Egypt") and functions to authenticate Moses and Aaron's Levite credentials at the point where they confront Pharaoh.
claims.evidence: the narrative break at 6:13/6:28 (text); the identification of the two men as the ones "to whom the LORD said" (6:26).

claims.claim: "Moses was fourscore years old, and Aaron fourscore and three years old, when they spake unto Pharaoh" (7:7). Clarke: Moses was 40 when he went to Midian and tarried 40 years there (Ex 2:11; Acts 7:30); Aaron was three years the elder.

"See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet" (7:1) — Moses as God's representative, Aaron as his spokesman (JFB: "interpreter"; Clarke: Aaron "shall receive the word from thy mouth").
claims.evidence: Ex 7:1; JFB and Clarke on Ex 7:1.

claims.claim: "And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt" (7:3). The hardening is announced before any plague falls.
"And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch forth mine hand upon Egypt" (7:5) — the stated purpose of the plagues, answering Pharaoh's "Who is the LORD?" (5:2).
Aaron casts down his rod and "it became a serpent" (7:10) — Hebrew *tannin*, not the *nachash* of Ex 4:3 (see clm-pl-023). The LXX renders it "dragon" (*drakōn*, 7:10, 12).
claims.evidence: Ex 7:9–10 (KJV); BDB via Clarke on Ex 7:10; NETS Ex 7:10, 12.

claims.claim: The rod at the burning bush became a *nachash* (Ex 4:3); before Pharaoh it becomes a *tannin* — the same word rendered "whale" in Gen 1:21. Clarke: from Ps 74:13; Isa 27:1; 51:9; Job 7:12, "some very large creature, either aquatic or amphibious... some have thought that the crocodile, a well-known Egyptian animal, is here intended."

Pharaoh calls "the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments" (7:11) — *chartummim*, "decipherers of abstruse writings" (Clarke, on Gen 41:8), working "with their enchantments" (*lahatim*, from *lahat*, "to burn" — incantations with lustral fires, Clarke). The names Jannes and Jambres for the chief magicians come only from 2 Tim 3:8 (traditional identification).
claims.evidence: Ex 7:11–12; BDB H2748; Clarke and JFB on Ex 7:11.

claims.claim: "But Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods" (7:12) — the sign of superiority that the magicians cannot match or undo (JFB: "what they could not be prepared for").

Two positions, both read directly, and no resolution: JFB argues for illusion and sleight of hand (modern Egyptian serpent-charmers who induce catalepsy by pressing the nape of the neck, making the serpent stiff as a rod, then producing it by legerdemain; the magicians "had time after the summons to make suitable preparations"); Clarke argues for familiar spirits ("there can be no doubt that real serpents were produced... by the ministry of a familiar spirit"). Jubilees 48:9–10 offers a third, ancient explanation (Mastema's help, permitted evils only).
claims.evidence: JFB and Clarke on Ex 7:11–12; Jubilees 48:9–10.

claims.claim: The KJV's "he hardened" renders the Hebrew *vayechezak lev Par'oh*, which Clarke notes is "the identical words which in Ex 7:22 are thus translated" as "the heart of Pharaoh was hardened," and argues it "should have been rendered in the same way here, lest the hardening... should be attributed to God." The Hebrew form is ambiguous between divine agency and a stative reading; the KJV's attribution of agency to God at 7:13 is a translation choice, not a textual datum.
claims.evidence: Ex 7:13, 22 (KJV); Clarke on Ex 7:13; BDB H2388.

claims.claim: The hardening is expressed by three distinct verbs: *chazaq* (H2388, "be or grow firm, strong"; Qal "grow stout, rigid, hard, with idea of perversity, of Pharaoh's heart," Ex 7:13, 22; 8:15; 9:35; Piel "make rigid, hard... harden (the heart)" with God as subject, Ex 4:21; 9:12; 10:20, 27; 11:10); *kaved* (H3513, "be heavy"; "heavy, insensible, dull, of the heart," Ex 9:7; Hiphil "make heavy, dull, unresponsive, the heart," Ex 8:11, 28; 9:34; 10:1); and *qashah* (H7185, "be hard, severe"; Hiphil "make hard, stiff, stubborn," Ex 7:3). The same root *kaved* yields God's "glory" (Niphal, "get oneself glory," Ex 14:4, 17, 18, "I will get me honour upon Pharaoh") — the heavy heart and the divine glory share one root, a probable wordplay.

In plagues 1–5 the hardening is stated without explicit divine agency (7:13, 22; 8:19; 9:7) or with Pharaoh as subject (8:15, 32; 9:34); from the sixth plague (boils, 9:12) God is the explicit subject ("the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh"), and divine hardening recurs at 10:1, 20, 27 and in the closing summary (11:10).
claims.evidence: the hardening verses across Ex 7–11 (KJV, read).

claims.claim: The announced hardening of 7:3 uses *qashah* (Hiphil, "I will harden," God as subject) — the only hardening verb in the chapter that is unambiguously divine in subject from the outset; it recurs of Pharaoh's own stubbornness at 13:15 ("Pharaoh made difficulty about sending us away").

(1) Clarke, permissive: "I will permit his stubbornness and obstinacy still to remain" (on 7:3); (2) JFB, resultative: "This would be the result. But the divine message would be the occasion, not the cause of the king's impenitent obduracy" (on 7:3); (3) Calvin, sovereign appointment: on 9:16, *he'emadti* "properly signifies 'to appoint'" — God placed Pharaoh on the throne, or preserved him, so His power might be displayed (on Rom 9:17, the predestination of Pharaoh to ruin "that he might exhibit a more illustrious evidence of His own power"). All three positions are documented in sources read for this dossier; none is adopted here.
claims.evidence: Clarke on Ex 7:3; JFB on Ex 7:3; Calvin on Ex 9:16 and Rom 9:17. Flagged for the EM (see Flags).

claims.claim: The Septuagint mirrors the Hebrew's variety: *ischyō* ("prevailed," 7:13), *barynō* ("weighed down/made heavy," 7:14; 8:32), *sklērynō* ("hardened," 7:22; 9:12).

Paul quotes Ex 9:16 as "Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee" (Rom 9:17), following the LXX's *exēgeira se* ("I have raised thee up") rather than the LXX's own *dietērēthēs* ("thou hast been preserved") at Ex 9:16 — a point Calvin notes on Rom 9:17 ("Paul changed the verb; for 'preserve,' used by the Septuagint, did not fully express the meaning").
claims.evidence: Rom 9:17; Ex 9:16 (KJV, NETS); Calvin on Rom 9:17.

claims.claim: Aaron stretches his rod over "the waters of Egypt, upon their streams, upon their rivers, and upon their ponds, and upon all their pools of water," and there is blood "throughout all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood, and in vessels of stone" (7:19–20); the fish die, the river stinks, and the Egyptians cannot drink (7:21). The magicians "did so with their enchantments" (7:22) — JFB: on a small scale, since the only drinkable water was dug from the sands, "on a sample or specimen of water dyed red."
"And seven days were fulfilled, after that the LORD had smitten the river" (7:25) — the only plague whose duration the text states.

The first plague strikes the river the Egyptians worshipped (Plutarch, *De Iside*, quoted by Clarke: "nothing is in greater honor among the Egyptians than the river Nile"; JFB: the Nile as "the patron deity of the country," and the plague as "a severe calamity" precisely because the river was the national god and the fish a staple food). The text itself names no Egyptian god; the identification is interpretive.
claims.evidence: Clarke on Ex 7:15; JFB on Ex 7:15, 17–21.

claims.claim: The river brings up frogs into houses, bedrooms, beds, ovens, and kneadingtroughs (8:3–4). Pharaoh begs intercession and names the time himself — "To morrow" (8:8–10) — and Moses answers, "Be it according to thy word: that thou mayest know that there is none like unto the LORD our God" (8:10).
The magicians "did so with their enchantments, and brought up frogs" (8:7); when Moses prays, the frogs die, "and they gathered them together upon heaps: and the land stank" (8:14).

The third plague is *kinnim* (8:16–17), from the dust of the earth, on man and beast. BDB: "meaning dubious; either gnat, gnats, gnat-swarm (so LXX, Vulgate, Philo *Vita Mos.* i, Josephus *Ant.* ii.14.3, Origen, and most moderns), or [louse,] lice (so Targum, Peshitta...)." The KJV's "lice" and the NASB's "gnats" both have ancient support; the LXX reads "gnats" (*skniphes*). The species cannot be fixed from the Hebrew.
claims.evidence: Ex 8:16–18; BDB H3654; NETS Ex 8:16–19. Flagged for Dev 2's prose (see Flags).

claims.claim: The magicians try "with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not" (8:18); "Then the magicians said unto Pharaoh, This is the finger of God" (8:19) — the first admission of divine agency, and the only Old Testament instance of the phrase spoken by a non-Israelite.

The third plague comes with no warning to Pharaoh and no prior audience (8:16) — the first of K&D's unannounced triad (3rd, 6th, 9th). The unannounced fact is textual; the triad pattern is K&D's structural observation.

The fourth plague is *'arov* (8:21–24), BDB "probably swarm (mixture)... of plague of stinging flies"; the KJV's "flies" is supplied (bracketed); the LXX renders it "dog-fly" (*kynomyia*); Philo describes the *kynomyia* at length. The Hebrew does not name a species.
claims.evidence: Ex 8:20–24; BDB H6157; NETS Ex 8:20–24; Philo, *Mos.* I.

claims.claim: "And I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth" (8:22–23). The first three plagues fell on Israel as well; from the fourth the distinction is explicit and repeated (9:4, 26; 10:23; 11:7).

Moses refuses Pharaoh's compromise ("sacrifice in the land," 8:25) because "we shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians to the LORD our God" (8:26) — the animals Egyptians held sacred; "if we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us?" The identification of the "abomination" with sacred animals is the standard reading.

Pharaoh concedes "I will let you go... only ye shall not go very far away" (8:28); Moses prays, the flies depart "and there remained not one" (8:31); "Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also" (8:32). The pattern of concession-on-affliction and retraction-on-relief is set.

"Behold, the hand of the LORD is upon thy cattle which is in the field... and there shall be a very grievous murrain" (9:3); "all the cattle of Egypt died" (9:6) — yet cattle remain in the field later (9:19–20, 25). K&D: the "all" is popular usage, the cattle in the field only; the livestock in stalls survived.

"Of the cattle of the children of Israel died not one" (9:6); "Pharaoh sent, and, behold, there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead" (9:7) — the only plague where Pharaoh sends to verify the distinction, and still will not let the people go.
claims.evidence: Ex 9:6–7; Calvin on Ex 9:7 (Pharaoh "deliberately passed over what it was very useful for him to know" until compelled to inspect).

claims.claim: Moses and Aaron take "handfuls of ashes of the furnace" and Moses sprinkles them toward heaven; they become "a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast" (9:8–10); "the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians, and upon all the Egyptians" (9:11). *Shechin*, from a root probably meaning "to burn" (BDB H7822); K&D's natural substratum is the Nile-blisters (*Hamm el Nil*).
claims.evidence: Ex 9:8–11; BDB H7822; K&D on Ex 9.

claims.claim: "And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he hearkened not unto them" (9:12) — the first hardening verse with God as explicit subject (see clm-pl-029).

"For I will at this time send all my plagues upon thine heart... that thou mayest know that there is none like me in all the earth. And in very deed for this cause have I raised thee up, for to shew in thee my power; and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth" (9:14–16). "And the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt... and the fire ran along upon the ground" (9:23–24); the LXX: "fire flashing in the hail" (9:24). *He'emadti* ("raised thee up") is variously rendered "appointed" / "preserved" / "stirred up" (Calvin on 9:16; see clm-pl-031).

"He that feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh made his servants and his cattle flee into the houses" (9:20); "he that regarded not the word of the LORD left his servants and his cattle in the field" (9:21). Some Egyptians heed the warning — the first Egyptians in the narrative who do.

"And the flax and the barley was smitten: for the barley was in the ear, and the flax was bolled. But the wheat and the rye were not smitten: for they were not grown up" (9:31–32) — a seasonal indicator (late winter/early spring) and the reason the locusts still have something to eat (10:5, 12, 15).

Pharaoh confesses, "I have sinned this time: the LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked" (9:27) and begs intercession (9:28); Moses prays, the hail ceases — and "when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunders were ceased, he sinned yet more, and hardened his heart" (9:34).

"That thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son, and of thy son's son, what things I have wrought in Egypt, and my signs which I have done among them; that ye may know how that I am the LORD" (10:2) — the second stated purpose of the plagues (with recognition, clm-pl-021/065).

Pharaoh's servants warn, "how long shall this man be a snare unto us? ... knowest thou not yet that Egypt is destroyed?" (10:7). Pharaoh offers the men alone — "Go now ye that are men" (10:11) — and Moses refuses a partial exodus. After the locusts, Pharaoh confesses, "I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you... forgive, I pray thee, my sin only this once" (10:16–17).

"The LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day, and all that night; and when it was morning, the east wind brought the locusts" (10:13); a "mighty strong west wind" takes them away and casts them "into the Red sea" (10:19).

"Darkness which may be felt" covers Egypt three days (10:21–22); "they saw not one another, neither rose any from his place for three days: but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings" (10:23). The LXX expands to "darkness, gloom, hurricane" (NETS, 10:22).
claims.evidence: Ex 10:21–23; NETS Ex 10:22 (and the NETS introduction's note on the expansion).

claims.claim: Pharaoh's final terms — "Go ye, serve the LORD; only let your flocks and your herds be stayed" (10:24) — are refused: "our cattle also shall go with us; there shall not an hoof be left behind" (10:26). Pharaoh ends the audiences: "Get thee from me... see my face no more" (10:28); Moses answers, "I will see thy face again no more" (10:29).

"Yet will I bring one plague more upon Pharaoh, and upon Egypt" (11:1); at midnight every firstborn in Egypt shall die, "from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne, even unto the firstborn of the maidservant that is behind the mill; and all the firstborn of beasts" (11:5). K&D reads 11:1 as pluperfect ("the LORD *had* said") — the announcement predating the last interview, with 11:4–8 recounting what Moses then said to Pharaoh. The pluperfect reading is K&D's grammatical judgment.

"But against any of the children of Israel shall not a dog move his tongue, against man or beast: that ye may know how that the LORD doth put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel" (11:7); "And he went out from Pharaoh in a great anger" (11:8). The closing summary (11:9–10) attributes the final hardening to the LORD.
The narrative describes ten plagues; it never numbers them, and the count is traditional in Jewish and Christian use (Bible Odyssey).
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, "The Plagues of Egypt"; the absence of any numbering in Ex 7–11.

claims.claim: K&D's arrangement: three triads (1–3, 4–6, 7–9); the 1st/2nd, 4th/5th, 7th/8th announced beforehand and the 3rd/6th/9th unannounced; the 1st/4th/7th announced in the morning; the first three falling on Israel as well; the last three the most dreadful. The Bible Odyssey article notes the same structural option (pairs, or three groups of three minus the final plague) while cautioning it "could also be the result of later editing."
claims.evidence: K&D on Ex 7–10 (triad structure); Bible Odyssey.

claims.claim: Philo divides the ten by element and minister: three by Aaron (earth and water — blood, frogs, lice), three by Moses (air and fire — hail, locusts, darkness), one by both (boils), three by God alone (dog-fly, cattle murrain, firstborn). Philo reorders the plagues to fit the elements; his scheme is interpretive, not a report of the narrative order.

The narrative's own term for the plagues is "signs and wonders" (*'otot u-moftim*, 7:3); *mopheth* is, in Clarke's definition, "an effect produced in nature which is opposed to its laws, or such as its powers are inadequate to produce" (on 7:9).
claims.evidence: Ex 7:3, 9; Clarke on Ex 7:9; Bible Odyssey (opening observation).

claims.claim: The plagues serve (1) recognition — "that thou mayest know that I am the LORD" (7:5, 17; 8:10, 22; 9:14, 29; 10:2; 11:7) and "that my name may be declared throughout all the earth" (9:16); and (2) memorial — "that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son" (10:2; cf. 12:26–27; 13:8, 14).

Outside Exodus, Ps 78:43–51 and Ps 105:28–36 each recount the plagues — but each lists only seven, and both differ from the order in Exodus (Ps 105 begins with darkness). The ten-plague list is not the only biblical form of the tradition.

The popular reading that each plague confronts a specific Egyptian god (Nile gods, land gods, sky gods) is **debated**: the Bible Odyssey article judges that "attempts to identify specific Egyptian gods behind the various plagues also falter, given the vague nature of the story where details regarding Egyptian religion are concerned." The general claim — that the plagues demonstrate YHWH's supremacy over Egypt's gods (JFB on 7:15; K&D) — is secure; the one-to-one identifications are not.

Ecological (Nile), volcanic, and cometary explanations of the plagues have been offered for half a century; the Bible Odyssey article's judgment is that "such correlations are highly speculative and, more importantly, lack any support in ancient Egyptian records relating to the Nile," and that naturalistic readings "ignore the literary or story-like nature of the narrative... as well as its clear miraculous intent." The Mesopotamian treaty-curse parallels (boils, locusts, disease, darkness, death of firstborn) and the water-to-blood omen motif show the motifs are not unique to Exodus.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey. (The Mesopotamian parallels are the article's report, not independently verified — see §5.7.)

claims.claim: K&D's observation that the plagues "are based on Egyptian natural phenomena, made signs by their excess and accumulation" — the Nile's reddening, the frogs of the inundation, the dust-gnats, the Nile-blisters, the rare hail, the east-wind locusts, the Chamsin darkness — describes the phenomena's Egyptian setting, not a naturalistic reduction.

The tenth plague differs in purpose and form from the nine: it is a direct judgment by God, not mediated through a natural occurrence (K&D). The announcement (Ex 11) already marks it off: it is the only plague announced as "one plague more" after the sequence is complete, and the only one whose execution is deferred to the next category.

Josephus retells the return (with Moses' Ethiopian campaign), the rod contest, the increased burden, and the ten plagues — in his order: blood (the river "sweet and fit for drinking to the Hebrews"), frogs, lice ("out of the bodies of the Egyptians"), a merged fourth plague of "pestilential creatures" followed by a distemper (flies and murrain compressed into one), boils, hail, locusts, darkness, firstborn. His "ten" are therefore not Exodus's ten, and his order must not be imported into the category prose. His stated purpose is apologetic: to show Moses "did not fail in any one thing that he foretold them" (2.14.1).

Jubilees lists the ten plagues in Exodus's order (blood, frogs, lice, dog-flies, boils, cattle death, hail, locusts, darkness, firstborn of men and animals) and adds that "on all their idols the Lord took vengeance and burned them with fire" (48:5). Mastema seeks to slay Moses on the way (48:2–3), helps the Egyptian sorcerers — "the evils indeed we permitted them to work, but the remedies we did not allow to be wrought by their hands" (48:9–10) — and "hardened their hearts" (48:17) so Egypt would pursue Israel.

Augustine's summary: Moses "overcame the *magi* of Pharaoh"; "ten memorable plagues were brought by Him upon them — the water turned into blood, the frogs and lice, the flies, the death of the cattle, the boils, the hail, the locusts, the darkness, the death of the first-born." He adds that Pharaoh is "the name of all the kings of Egypt" and counts 144 years from Joseph's death to the Exodus (his own chronology, not the text's). He closes with the Finger of God as the Holy Spirit, connecting Ex 8:19 with Ex 31:18. **Correction:** the Phase 0 plan's "XVI.27–43" is wrong — chs. 27–42 are Abraham–Joseph; the Exodus material is ch. 43 (with an incidental mention in ch. 6).
claims.evidence: Augustine, *City of God* XVI.6, XVI.43 (Dods, New Advent; read directly).

claims.claim: Philo's central observations: water is struck first because Egyptians honoured water as the first principle; the lice show God admonishing through insignificant agents ("what can be more insignificant than a louse?"); Israel is untouched by every plague "though dwelling in the same houses" — the same events destroy one people and preserve the other.
claims.evidence: Philo, *De vita Mosis* I.96–146 (Yonge; read directly).

claims.claim: The *Admonitions of Ipuwer* (Papyrus Leiden I 344) is a New Kingdom copy of a Middle Kingdom composition, translated by Alan H. Gardiner in 1909 (*The Admonitions of an Egyptian Sage from a Hieratic Papyrus in Leiden*). Ipuwer is generally supposed to have lived in the Middle Kingdom or Second Intermediate Period, with the catastrophes placed four centuries earlier in the First Intermediate Period.
claims.evidence: Gardiner 1909 (as reproduced and framed on holykosher.com); Lichtheim, *Ancient Egyptian Literature* I, p. 150 (as quoted there — **second-hand**).

claims.claim: Gardiner's translation contains genuine verbal resemblances to the plague narrative: "Plague is throughout the land. Blood is everywhere" (2:5–6); "Indeed, the river is blood, yet men drink of it. Men shrink from human beings and thirst after water" (2:10); "gates, columns and walls are burnt up" (2:10); "grain has perished on every side" (6:3); "that has perished which yesterday was seen, and the land is left over to its weakness like the cutting of flax" (5:12); "the children of princes are dashed against walls" (4:3); gold and silver "fastened on the neck of female slaves" (3:2).
claims.evidence: Ipuwer, Gardiner translation (read directly via the holykosher reproduction).

claims.claim: Ipuwer is a lament over social inversion — the poor enriched, slaves taking their masters' goods, barbarians invading, trade ceasing, the king absent — with no Moses, no Pharaoh confronted, no Israel, no tenfold sequence, no divine agent, and no deliverance. The "blood" of 2:10 sits in a passage about corpses in the river ("many dead are buried in the river; the stream is a sepulcher"), and the fire is the burning of cities in civil strife.

Lichtheim (following Luria): the *Admonitions* "has not only no bearing whatever on the long past First Intermediate Period, it also does not derive from any other historical situation. It is the last, fullest, most exaggerated and hence least successful, composition on the theme 'order versus chaos.'" The mainstream scholarly position is that Ipuwer is a literary lament, not a historical record of the plagues; the identification with the Exodus is maintained chiefly in popular and apologetic literature (e.g. Becher; Aaronson, *Jewish Action*, Spring 1995).
claims.evidence: Lichtheim as quoted (second-hand via the holykosher reproduction); the holykosher framing; §5.2. Per the brief, any claim citing Ipuwer is Debated at best.

claims.claim: The Exodus narrative names no Pharaoh and gives no date for the plagues.
claims.evidence: Ex 5–11 (the absence is verifiable in the text read).

claims.claim: From 1 Kings 6:1 (480 years before Solomon's fourth year, c. 966 BCE), the Exodus is computed to c. 1446 BCE, under a Pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty (Thutmose III or Amenhotep II are the usual candidates). The 480-year figure is in the text; the resulting date is a computation and is debated.
claims.evidence: 1 Kgs 6:1; BiblicalTraining's summary of the dating debate.

claims.claim: The 13th-century dating (Ramesses II) rests principally on Ex 1:11, the store-city "Raamses," a name fitting the 19th Dynasty capital Pi-Ramesses. It is a live scholarly position, not established by the text; the name could be anachronistic or updated.
claims.evidence: Ex 1:11; the dating debate as summarised in the sources read.

claims.claim: The Merneptah Stele (year 5, c. 1209 BCE) records "Israel is laid waste, its seed is not" (line 27) — the earliest extrabiblical reference to Israel, with the determinative of a people, not a city or land. Israel therefore already existed as a people in Canaan by c. 1209 BCE; both datings satisfy this constraint, and the stele fixes nothing more precise.
claims.evidence: Merneptah Stele, line 27 (ANET 378; Hoffmeier's rendering, as quoted in the Wikipedia article and the Lexham summary, read directly — **second-hand**).

claims.claim: JFB lists three candidate locations for Pharaoh's court: Rameses, Memphis, or Tanis "in the field of Zoan" (Ps 78:12). The text does not say.
Ussher dated the ten plagues within a single month (18th day of the sixth month to 15th Abib), as reported by Clarke on Ex 7:17; Clarke himself: "most of these dates are destitute of proof."
Ex 9:31–32 (flax and barley smitten, wheat and rye not yet grown) indicates late winter or early spring.

Ex 6:9 ("anguish of spirit") ↔ Ex 5:21 (the people's complaint against Moses and Aaron). The renewed promise meets the despair the first audience produced.

Ex 7:1 ("I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet") ↔ Ex 4:16 ("he shall be thy spokesman unto the people, and... thou shalt be to him instead of God"). The same Moses–Aaron–God relationship, stated from the other side.
Ex 7:3 ("I will harden Pharaoh's heart") ↔ Ex 4:21 (the same announcement at the burning bush). The Midian commission and the Egyptian commission agree.
Ex 7:7 (Moses 80) ↔ Acts 7:30 ("when forty years were expired, there appeared to him in the wilderness of mount Sina an angel of the Lord"). The age implies the forty-year sojourn.
Ex 7:9–10 (*tannin*) ↔ Ex 4:3 (*nachash*). The sign is the same; the word changes.
Ex 7:11 (the magicians, unnamed) ↔ 2 Tim 3:8 ("Jannes and Jambres... withstood Moses"). The New Testament supplies the traditional names.

Ex 8:19 ("This is the finger of God") ↔ Ex 31:18 (the tables "written with the finger of God") and Luke 11:20 ("if I with the finger of God cast out devils"). The phrase links the plagues, the law, and Jesus' exorcisms; Augustine makes the same connection (*City of God* XVI.43).
Ex 7:17 ("In this thou shalt know that I am the LORD") ↔ Ex 9:14 ("that thou mayest know that there is none like me in all the earth"). The formula recurs at each escalation.

Ex 10:7 ("knowest thou not yet that Egypt is destroyed?") ↔ Ex 12:33 ("the Egyptians were urgent upon the people... for they said, We be all dead men"). The servants' warning is fulfilled at the departure.
Ex 10:23 ("all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings") ↔ Ex 14:20 (the pillar of cloud is darkness to the Egyptians and light to Israel). The same contrast at the sea.
Ex 11:1 ("Yet will I bring one plague more") ↔ Ex 12:29–30 (its execution). The announcement belongs to this category; the execution to the next.
Ex 11:5 (every firstborn in Egypt shall die) ↔ Ex 4:22–23 ("Israel is my son, even my firstborn... I will slay thy son, even thy firstborn"). The threat made at the bush is executed at the Passover.
Ex 11:7 ↔ Josh 10:21 ("none moved his tongue against any of the children of Israel"). The phrase recurs at the conquest's completion.
Ex 11:8 ("he went out from Pharaoh in a great anger") ↔ Ex 32:19 (Moses' anger at the golden calf). The anger that leaves Pharaoh's court returns at Sinai.

Ex 5:9 ("let there more work be laid upon the men" — *kaved*) ↔ Ex 7:14 ("Pharaoh's heart is hardened" — *kaved*). The same root describes the burden laid on Israel and the hardness of Pharaoh's heart; and the same root yields God's "glory" (Ex 14:4).

Ex 6:6 ("I will redeem you with a stretched out arm") ↔ Ex 15:13 ("thou in thy mercy hast led forth the people which thou hast redeemed"). The redemption promised before the plagues is sung after the sea.
Ex 7:3 ("my signs and my wonders") ↔ Deut 6:22 ("the LORD shewed signs and wonders, great and sore, upon Egypt, before our eyes"). Deuteronomy remembers the plagues in the narrative's own terms.
